info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 12.2: Deterministic Intertextual Discovery and Linked Web Annotation.

name.text: 01 Question: The Algorithmic Search for Text Reuse

questiontext.text: Why do scholars use deterministic algorithms to search for text reuse across historical archives?

generalfeedback.text: rule-based text reuse algorithms scan vast document collections using fixed rules to discover shared phrases and citations beyond human memory.

answer.text: They scan vast document collections using fixed rules to discover shared phrases and citations beyond human memory limits.

feedback.text: Correct. Deterministic algorithms run predictable, rule-based operations that never hallucinate, surfacing connections humans miss.

answer.text: They rewrite historical documents into modern slang automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text reuse algorithms detect shared phrasing, not slang rewriting.

answer.text: They delete older archival documents to free up server hard drive space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Algorithms preserve and analyze historical texts, never delete them.

answer.text: They replace human historians with automated robots that grade student papers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text discovery tools assist scholars with discovery rather than replacing scholarly evaluation.

name.text: 02 Question: The Mechanics of Text Reuse: word vs. sentence

questiontext.text: What is the difference between verbatim text reuse and modified text reuse in historical documents?

generalfeedback.text: Text reuse ranges from verbatim copying to modified summary, requiring different algorithmic detection strategies.

answer.text: Verbatim reuse is exact, word-for-word repetition, while modified reuse adapts language through paraphrase, word order changes, or omission.

feedback.text: Correct. Verbatim loans are easily detected by string matching, whereas modified reuse requires proximity scoring and lemmatization.

answer.text: Verbatim reuse occurs only in poetry, while modified reuse occurs only in legal statutes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both forms of text reuse occur across all genres of historical writing.

answer.text: Verbatim reuse is always illegal plagiarism, while modified reuse is always authorized.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical text reuse was a standard scribal and legal drafting practice, not modern copyright infringement.

answer.text: Verbatim reuse changes the language, while modified reuse keeps all characters identical.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This completely reverses the definitions.

name.text: 03 Question: The Tesserae Framework: Principles of text-linking Discovery

questiontext.text: How does the Tesserae framework discover text reuse between historical texts?

generalfeedback.text: The Tesserae framework discovers text reuse by scoring the pairing of shared words based on rarity and physical proximity.

answer.text: By identifying and scoring sentence pairs that share two or more rare vocabulary words within a close textual window.

feedback.text: Correct. Tesserae calculates match scores based on word rarity and physical proximity between shared terms.

answer.text: By comparing the color and chemical composition of the ink on digitized manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tesserae analyzes digital text strings, not physical chemical ink properties.

answer.text: By translating both documents into classical Greek and counting the syllables.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tesserae operates directly on the target vocabulary of the texts.

answer.text: By asking human volunteers to vote on which text is more beautifully written.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tesserae is an automated computational algorithm, not a crowd-sourced voting platform.

name.text: 04 Question: Preprocessing: Stoplists and Normalization

questiontext.text: Why must editors apply a stoplist before running text reuse algorithms on primary documents?

generalfeedback.text: Preprocessing historical text through case folding, punctuation removal, and stoplists is essential for finding meaningful text reuse.

answer.text: To filter out ubiquitous grammatical words (like 'the', 'and', 'in') that would otherwise cause every sentence to match by accident.

feedback.text: Correct. Removing high-frequency stopwords prevents false matches and forces the algorithm to focus on meaningful content words.

answer.text: To delete all swear words from historical manuscripts before students read them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A stoplist filters high-frequency function words, not offensive language.

answer.text: To prevent unauthorized users from downloading the document from GitHub.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stoplists are data preprocessing tools, not security access controls.

answer.text: Because XML parsers crash if they encounter the word 'the'.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsers process common words without difficulty.

name.text: 05 Question: Word Rarity and TF-IDF Weighting

questiontext.text: In the TF-IDF statistical weighting formula, how does Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) help identify important text parallels?

generalfeedback.text: TF-IDF weighting mathematically models scholarly intuition by prioritizing rare, distinctive terms over ubiquitous vocabulary.

answer.text: It assigns high numerical weights to rare terms while discounting common words that appear across the entire corpus.

feedback.text: Correct. IDF ensures that specialized legal terms like 'Truckhouse' score much higher than generic words like 'governor'.

answer.text: It counts the total number of pages in the printed book.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IDF evaluates vocabulary rarity across documents, not physical page counts.

answer.text: It measures how fast the user can type words on a keyboard.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IDF is an algorithmic text analysis metric, not a human typing test.

answer.text: It deletes any word that appears fewer than three times in the document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IDF boosts rare words rather than deleting them.

name.text: 06 Question: Distance Scoring: Word Proximity

questiontext.text: Why do intertextual discovery algorithms apply a proximity penalty when matching words in a candidate passage?

generalfeedback.text: Measuring word proximity ensures that algorithms prioritize compact, formulaic phrases over accidental, distant word pairings.

answer.text: Words appearing close together in a compact phrase indicate intentional borrowing, while words spread far apart are often coincidental.

feedback.text: Correct. Compact phrase density is a strong indicator of formulaic legal text reuse or direct quotation.

answer.text: Because computer memory runs out if words are more than ten inches apart on screen.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Proximity scoring is an analytical heuristic, not a memory hardware constraint.

answer.text: To force historical authors to write shorter sentences in the future.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Algorithms analyze historical text as written; they cannot alter past authors.

answer.text: Because long sentences are forbidden in digital editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital editions accommodate historical sentences of any length.

name.text: 07 Question: Precision vs. Recall in Algorithmic Discovery

questiontext.text: When configuring an automated text reuse tool, what happens if an editor sets the match threshold for extremely high precision?

generalfeedback.text: Editorial tool configuration balances precision against recall, trading off between missing subtle parallels and filtering out false alarms.

answer.text: The tool returns almost exclusively genuine historical parallels, but misses many subtle or modified borrowings (false negatives).

feedback.text: Correct. High precision minimizes false alarms at the expense of lower recall, missing modified or paraphrased text reuse.

answer.text: The tool crashes the computer and deletes all project files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Changing match thresholds adjusts search stringency without crashing systems.

answer.text: The tool captures 100% of all parallels with zero missed items.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Capturing all parallels describes high recall, which typically lowers precision.

answer.text: The tool begins generating fictional hallucinations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deterministic algorithms run fixed mathematical rules and never hallucinate.

name.text: 08 Question: What rule-based Algorithms Catch

questiontext.text: Which type of textual connection are deterministic algorithms most effective at detecting across historical corpora?

generalfeedback.text: rule-based tools excel at surfacing verbatim legal formulas, commercial boilerplate, and direct legal cross-references.

answer.text: Verbatim statutory formulas, standardized treaty articles, and identical commercial boilerplate.

feedback.text: Correct. Deterministic tools excel at surfacing exact lexical repetitions that span across large archival collections.

answer.text: Subtle psychological motivations of historical figures.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Psychological motivations require deep historical interpretation, not string matching.

answer.text: Ironic literary metaphors that contain no shared vocabulary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Algorithms cannot detect metaphors that share zero vocabulary.

answer.text: Predictions of 21st-century technological inventions in 18th-century treaties.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical documents do not predict future technologies.

name.text: 09 Question: What rule-based Algorithms Miss

questiontext.text: Why do deterministic word-matching algorithms fail to detect conceptual allusions and paraphrases?

generalfeedback.text: rule-based tools are blind to synonyms, conceptual allusions, and spelling variations, requiring human oversight to catch missed connections.

answer.text: They match literal character strings and lemmas, making them blind to synonym substitutions, structural metaphors, and conceptual echoes.

feedback.text: Correct. If an author expresses the same idea using different words, simple string matching algorithms see zero connection.

answer.text: Because digital computers are not permitted to read historical literature.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computers can process literature, but string algorithms lack semantic comprehension.

answer.text: Because all historical authors wrote in secret encrypted code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Archival documents were written in standard natural languages of their era.

answer.text: Because algorithms only operate on numbers, not text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. String algorithms process text characters directly.

name.text: 10 Question: Auditing Algorithmic Output Against Tuesday's Ground Truth

questiontext.text: In the three-step comparative cycle, how does auditing algorithmic results against Tuesday's manual notes advance your research?

generalfeedback.text: Auditing algorithmic results against manual ground truth reveals tool strengths, uncovers missed parallels, and identifies false positives.

answer.text: It reveals whether the algorithm validated your hand-crafted discoveries, identifies newly surfaced true parallels, and tallies false alarms.

feedback.text: Correct. Benchmarking against ground truth allows scholars to measure algorithmic precision and identify blind spots.

answer.text: It allows students to discard their primary sources and submit computer code instead.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The primary sources remain the foundation of the edition.

answer.text: It proves that human scholars should never read primary sources manually.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual reading creates the ground truth benchmark that makes evaluation possible.

answer.text: It changes the date of the historical treaty in official government archives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Auditing digital tools has no effect on historical chronology.

name.text: 11 Question: Beyond the Local File: The Need for Web Annotation

questiontext.text: Why did the scholarly community develop international web annotation standards beyond local TEI XML standoff files?

generalfeedback.text: Web annotation standards allow scholars to attach commentary to remote archival images and texts across the internet without altering host servers.

answer.text: To allow scholars to attach commentary to remote archival scans and web pages without requiring write access to the host museum servers.

feedback.text: Correct. Web annotation decouples notes from host server storage, allowing decentralized commentary across the public internet.

answer.text: Because TEI XML was permanently banned by the United Nations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML remains the premier international standard for text encoding.

answer.text: To force all digital editions to be viewed exclusively on mobile phones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web standards ensure device independence across all platforms.

answer.text: Because local hard drives cannot store more than five annotations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Local storage capacity is not the issue; cross-institutional sharing is.

name.text: 12 Question: The W3C Web Annotation Data Model

questiontext.text: What are the three core structural components of every annotation in the W3C Web Annotation Data Model?

generalfeedback.text: The W3C Web Annotation Data Model structures commentary into three universal components: the Annotation, the Target, and the Body.

answer.text: The Annotation container, the Target (what is being annotated), and the Body (what the annotation says).

feedback.text: Correct. The W3C specification structures every annotation into Annotation, Target, and Body.

answer.text: The Header, the Paragraph, and the Footer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These describe traditional HTML document layout sections.

answer.text: The Username, the Password, and the Credit Card.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are e-commerce authentication fields.

answer.text: The Input, the Processor, and the Output.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These describe general computing architecture.

name.text: 13 Question: JSON-LD: The Language of Web Annotations

questiontext.text: In a W3C Web Annotation serialized in JSON-LD, what is the role of the @context property?

generalfeedback.text: JSON-LD serializes W3C Web Annotations into a web-native, machine-readable format that connects commentary to live URLs.

answer.text: It links property names to standardized W3C linked data vocabularies, ensuring that web software interprets keys like 'body' and 'target' correctly.

feedback.text: Correct. The @context declaration provides the semantic schema mapping that turns plain JSON into Linked Open Data.

answer.text: It hides the author's email address from computer hackers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. @context defines ontology mappings, not user privacy settings.

answer.text: It automatically translates the note into seven different foreign languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. @context maps data keys, not human language translations.

answer.text: It tells the web browser to delete the file after twenty-four hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web annotations are persistent data objects.

name.text: 14 Question: The W3C Motivation Taxonomy

questiontext.text: Which W3C motivation should be assigned to an annotation that attaches an external authority record to a person or place?

generalfeedback.text: Specifying a W3C motivation (`commenting`, `identifying`, `linking`) clarifies the scholarly purpose of each digital note for web software.

answer.text: motivation: 'identifying'

feedback.text: Correct. The 'identifying' motivation signals that the annotation attaches an authoritative identity or gazetteer record to a textual entity.

answer.text: motivation: 'bookmarking'

feedback.text: Incorrect. 'Bookmarking' records a location for future reading, not authority identification.

answer.text: motivation: 'moderating'

feedback.text: Incorrect. 'Moderating' evaluates forum comment quality, not entity authority linking.

answer.text: motivation: 'questioning'

feedback.text: Incorrect. 'Questioning' raises doubts or queries, whereas authority tagging identifies entities.

name.text: 15 Question: The Anchoring Problem on the Dynamic Web

questiontext.text: Why are raw character offsets especially unreliable for anchoring annotations on public web pages?

generalfeedback.text: Web annotations require resilient selectors to ensure notes stay attached to target text even when website layouts are updated.

answer.text: Website redesigns, template updates, and text revisions constantly shift character positions, causing notes to attach to the wrong text or disappear.

feedback.text: Correct. Dynamic web pages change frequently, making fragile character counts obsolete upon any layout update.

answer.text: Because web browsers cannot count characters higher than ten.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Browsers process millions of characters, but DOM positions shift during edits.

answer.text: Because the W3C strictly outlaws using numbers on web pages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Numbers are standard data types in all web protocols.

answer.text: Because character offsets cause computer screens to flicker.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Anchor fragility is a data consistency problem, not a visual display glitch.

name.text: 16 Question: The TextQuoteSelector: Robust Text Anchoring

questiontext.text: How does the W3C TextQuoteSelector ensure that an annotation stays attached to its target text even if the webpage HTML changes?

generalfeedback.text: The `TextQuoteSelector` ensures annotations survive web redesigns by locking onto the target phrase and its surrounding context words.

answer.text: It records the exact target phrase along with its immediate prefix and suffix words, allowing software to search for and relocate the phrase in context.

feedback.text: Correct. The combination of prefix, exact text, and suffix disambiguates repeated phrases and survives surrounding HTML redesigns.

answer.text: It locks the remote museum server so that archivists cannot edit their own web pages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Annotations cannot lock or restrict remote server administration.

answer.text: It downloads the entire internet into a single text file on your laptop.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Selectors store small context strings, not entire websites.

answer.text: It converts the webpage into an uneditable paper printout.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web annotations operate dynamically within digital browsers.

name.text: 17 Question: Positional and Image Selectors

questiontext.text: Which W3C selector allows an editor to attach a commentary note to a specific visual region on a high-resolution digitized treaty scan?

generalfeedback.text: Image fragment selectors allow scholars to attach commentary directly to specific visual regions on digitized manuscript scans and photographs.

answer.text: FragmentSelector with spatial media fragment coordinates (e.g., xywh=160,240,400,120).

feedback.text: Correct. Spatial fragment selectors define rectangular bounding boxes on images and facsimiles conforming to media fragment standards.

answer.text: TextQuoteSelector without any image data.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text quote selectors match text strings, not pixel coordinates on image facsimiles.

answer.text: CSS FontSelector with color values.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Font selectors style typography, not spatial image coordinates.

answer.text: GPS GeolocationSelector for outdoor satellite tracking.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital image coordinates address pixel space on a canvas, not satellite GPS.

name.text: 18 Question: Selector Chains for Maximum Durability

questiontext.text: Why do robust web annotation platforms combine multiple selectors into an ordered selector chain?

generalfeedback.text: Combining positional lookups and text quote selectors into chains guarantees maximum durability for digital commentary on the web.

answer.text: To implement graceful degradation, attempting fast positional lookups first and falling back to resilient text quote matching if page edits occurred.

feedback.text: Correct. Selector chains maximize speed when pages are static and guarantee recovery when pages are modified.

answer.text: To confuse search engines so that competing universities cannot read the annotations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Selector chains enhance data recovery, not obfuscation.

answer.text: Because the W3C requires every annotation to be written in three different computer languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Selector chains are an anchoring resilience strategy within JSON-LD.

answer.text: To force users to click three times before viewing a note.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Selector chains execute automatically behind the scenes without extra clicks.

name.text: 19 Question: Collaborative Web Annotation with Hypothes.is

questiontext.text: How does the Hypothes.is platform operationalize W3C web annotation standards for classroom teaching?

generalfeedback.text: Platforms like Hypothes.is operationalize the W3C standard, allowing students and scholars to annotate live web pages and PDFs collaboratively.

answer.text: It allows students and instructors to highlight and annotate live web pages and online PDFs collaboratively, generating standard JSON-LD notes behind the scenes.

feedback.text: Correct. Hypothes.is provides an accessible browser overlay that generates W3C-compliant annotations across public websites and PDFs.

answer.text: It replaces the university library catalog with a private social media chat room.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hypothes.is is an academic annotation platform, not social media chat.

answer.text: It automatically grades student essays using generative artificial intelligence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hypothes.is is a human collaborative annotation tool, not an automated grading bot.

answer.text: It blocks all students from accessing historical archives online.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hypothes.is facilitates collaborative engagement with online archives.

name.text: 20 Question: Semantic Tagging and Authority Linking with Recogito

questiontext.text: What primary scholarly capability does the Recogito platform provide when annotating historical texts and maps?

generalfeedback.text: Recogito demonstrates how W3C web annotations connect textual mentions of places to interactive maps and global gazetteers.

answer.text: It allows editors to highlight place names, automatically queries global gazetteers like GeoNames, and plots historical entities on interactive maps.

feedback.text: Correct. Recogito links textual place mentions to geographic coordinates and visualizes them on interactive maps.

answer.text: It automatically purchases antique maps from online auction websites.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recogito is a scholarly research tool, not an e-commerce purchasing bot.

answer.text: It deletes all historical place names and replaces them with modern postal codes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recogito preserves historical toponyms while linking them to gazetteer records.

answer.text: It translates English documents into computer assembly code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recogito performs semantic annotation and geoparsing, not low-level code compilation.

name.text: 21 Question: Linked Open Data and Knowledge Graphs

questiontext.text: In a Linked Open Data knowledge graph, how are historical entities connected to one another?

generalfeedback.text: Linking annotations to global authorities integrates local student editions into a worldwide knowledge graph of historical data.

answer.text: Through subject-predicate-object semantic statements (triples) linking persistent URIs, such as Hopson [governed] Nova Scotia.

feedback.text: Correct. Knowledge graphs encode relationships between real-world entities using standardized RDF triples.

answer.text: By saving all historical documents in one giant Microsoft Excel spreadsheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Knowledge graphs use graph databases and linked data standards, not local flat spreadsheets.

answer.text: By printing paper cards and mailing them to the national archives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Linked Open Data is a decentralized digital web architecture.

answer.text: By ensuring that all historical figures have identical personal names.

feedback.text: Incorrect. URIs disambiguate figures with similar names, preserving distinct historical identities.

name.text: 22 Question: Querying Commentary Networks with SPARQL

questiontext.text: What is the primary role of the SPARQL query language in digital humanities research?

generalfeedback.text: SPARQL enables scholars to execute complex relational queries across distributed linked data networks and digital commentaries.

answer.text: It executes structured relational queries across distributed Linked Open Data graphs to extract specific historical entities and relationships.

feedback.text: Correct. SPARQL allows researchers to query complex RDF graphs across the web to answer multi-variable historical research questions.

answer.text: It formats text into decorative italic fonts in Microsoft Word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SPARQL is a semantic query language, not a word processor styling tool.

answer.text: It checks whether student laptops are connected to the university Wi-Fi network.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SPARQL queries databases, not campus network hardware.

answer.text: It deletes spam emails from the instructor's inbox automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SPARQL queries graph data, not email servers.

name.text: 23 Question: Comparing TEI Standoff XML vs. W3C JSON-LD

questiontext.text: Why do many digital publishing projects maintain their primary source edition in TEI XML while exporting annotations to W3C JSON-LD?

generalfeedback.text: TEI XML is ideal for archival textual editions, while W3C JSON-LD excels at web-native sharing and distributed annotation across remote servers.

answer.text: TEI XML provides rigorous archival validation for the primary text, while JSON-LD provides lightweight interoperability for interactive web browsers.

feedback.text: Correct. Combining TEI XML for archival depth with JSON-LD for web distribution leverages the unique strengths of both standards.

answer.text: Because TEI XML cannot be opened on computers made after 2010.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML is completely compatible with modern computing systems.

answer.text: Because JSON-LD files are completely immune to computer viruses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON-LD is a data serialization format; security depends on system architecture.

answer.text: Because universities require all student work to be stored in at least ten conflicting formats.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Combining complementary standards is a deliberate, reasoned architectural strategy.

name.text: 24 Question: Hands-On Exercise: Searching for Text Reuse in VS Code

questiontext.text: When searching for text reuse across your workspace in VS Code, what is the advantage of using regex proximity search over plain string search?

generalfeedback.text: Use VS Code multi-file and regex search to detect verbatim formulas and proximity matches across your project corpus.

answer.text: It allows you to find two meaningful words that appear near each other even if minor intervening words or punctuation differ.

feedback.text: Correct. Regex patterns like 'liberty\s+(?:\w+\s+){1,4}hunting' capture modified text reuse that exact string search misses.

answer.text: It automatically translates the document into medieval Latin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regex search queries local text; it does not translate languages.

answer.text: It turns off all computer security firewalls permanently.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text search within an editor has no impact on system firewalls.

answer.text: It guarantees that 100% of discovered matches are intentional plagiarisms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors must still evaluate whether discovered proximity matches represent genuine text reuse.

name.text: 25 Question: Hands-On Exercise: Converting a TEI Note to W3C JSON-LD

questiontext.text: When translating a TEI standoff note into a W3C Web Annotation JSON-LD object, where does the note text reside?

generalfeedback.text: Converting TEI standoff notes into W3C JSON-LD makes your commentary accessible to web browsers and external digital archives.

answer.text: Inside the 'body' property within a 'TextualBody' object.

feedback.text: Correct. The W3C specification places annotation comments inside the body property, typically with type 'TextualBody'.

answer.text: Inside the computer's operating system kernel.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Note data resides inside the JSON-LD data structure.

answer.text: In the filename of the computer hard drive partition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Textual content is encoded in the file body, not disk partition labels.

answer.text: Inside an invisible comment hidden from web browsers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The body is the primary visible content payload of the annotation.

name.text: 26 Question: Designing a rule-based Commentary Index Table

questiontext.text: What key metadata columns should be included in a commentary index table to enable efficient thematic browsing?

generalfeedback.text: A commentary index table organizes all edition notes into a clear directory with categories, headwords, and authority links.

answer.text: Note ID, Anchor Target, Category/Subtype, Headword/Topic, and External Authority Link.

feedback.text: Correct. These five columns provide a complete directory allowing readers to navigate notes by identifier, domain, topic, and linked data authority.

answer.text: Author's home address, social security number, and bank account balance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Private personal data must never be recorded in digital edition tables.

answer.text: Monitor refresh rate, keyboard serial number, and room temperature.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hardware metrics are irrelevant to scholarly commentary indexes.

answer.text: Three random numbers chosen by rolling dice.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commentary indexes require accurate, verified scholarly metadata.

name.text: 27 Question: Evaluating Candidate Matches: The Human Gatekeeper

questiontext.text: Why must editors apply a historical plausibility gate before accepting an algorithmic match into a scholarly commentary?

generalfeedback.text: Treat all algorithmic matches as proposals; apply strict historical plausibility and significance gates before accepting notes into your edition.

answer.text: To verify that the earlier text was historically accessible to the author, eliminating coincidental phrase overlaps that could not represent real influence.

feedback.text: Correct. An algorithm only knows that words match; human historians must verify whether historical contact and transmission were plausible.

answer.text: To ensure that the modern digital edition will never be criticized online.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Plausibility gates guarantee scholarly rigor, but do not prevent critique.

answer.text: Because copyright law requires all historical authors to sign digital consent forms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical texts from the 18th and 20th centuries do not require retrospective digital consent.

answer.text: To force the algorithm to run faster on modern computer processors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Evaluative gates are human intellectual reviews conducted after the algorithm runs.

name.text: 28 Question: Documenting rule-based Discoveries in COMMENTARY.md

questiontext.text: In your research ledger, why is it essential to distinguish between True Positives and False Positives in your algorithm results table?

generalfeedback.text: Record search strategies, true/false positive counts, and ground truth comparisons in `COMMENTARY.md` to document your algorithmic audit.

answer.text: It provides an honest, empirical measurement of algorithm precision, documenting which candidate matches were real connections and which were noise.

feedback.text: Correct. Tracking true vs false positives documents the efficacy and limitations of automated text reuse tools.

answer.text: It automatically deletes all false matches from the internet permanently.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ledgers record scholarly observations; they do not delete remote web data.

answer.text: It proves that computer algorithms are always completely useless.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Documenting precision demonstrates the complementary value of automated search alongside human vetting.

answer.text: It allows the student to avoid writing their final exam.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Research ledgers document laboratory milestones, not exam exemptions.

name.text: 29 Question: Preparing for Friday: The Shift to AI-Assisted Commentary

questiontext.text: What fundamental difference distinguishes generative large language models from deterministic search algorithms?

generalfeedback.text: rule-based tools provide predictable string matching, setting the stage for evaluating AI models that understand semantic context but risk factual hallucination.

answer.text: Language models understand semantic context and generate fluent prose, but carry a significant risk of hallucinating plausible-sounding falsehoods.

feedback.text: Correct. Generative AI excels at synthesizing context and fluency, but requires rigorous verification against hallucinations.

answer.text: Language models only work when disconnected from the internet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generative models operate through cloud APIs and local servers.

answer.text: Deterministic algorithms can think and feel emotions, while language models cannot.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neither tool possesses consciousness; deterministic tools follow fixed rules, while LLMs predict token distributions.

answer.text: Language models never make factual errors under any circumstances.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generative models frequently hallucinate fake citations and historical inaccuracies.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: The Complementarity of Tools

questiontext.text: How do manual scholarship, deterministic algorithms, and W3C web standards complement one another in digital edition design?

generalfeedback.text: Combining manual human depth, rule-based archival scale, and W3C web standards produces durable, connected digital scholarly editions.

answer.text: Manual research provides intellectual depth, deterministic tools provide archival scale, and web standards provide global interoperability.

feedback.text: Correct. Combining human depth, algorithmic scale, and open web standards produces resilient, world-class digital editions.

answer.text: They compete against one another until only one single tool survives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Different tools serve complementary functions within an integrated workflow.

answer.text: They allow editors to publish historical editions without reading the primary text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rigorous digital editing requires deep engagement with the primary witness.

answer.text: They ensure that no student ever needs to learn computer skills again.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern humanities scholarship integrates advanced digital and conceptual competencies.
